name: Troll's Gift Ring
powers: Gifts from the hidden folk bring luck to those who accept them without greed, and ruin to the grasping.
description: In Norwegian and Scandinavian folk belief, the hulder and the troll folk sometimes press gifts upon humans — rings, bracelets, or coins that look like gold. Accepting such a gift courteously could bring lasting luck, while greedily taking more, or refusing rudely, brought misfortune. The motif is widely told across Norway, Sweden, and Denmark, with many local variations on what the gift becomes at dawn.
source: Norwegian folk tradition (eventyr and sagn collections)

name: Tyrfing
aliases: The Cursed Sword of Hervarar saga
powers: Never misses and never rusts, but kills a man every time it is drawn and brings three great evils.
description: Cursed sword of the Hervarar saga, forged by the dwarves Dvalinn and Dulinn for King Svafrlami, whom they cursed in return: the blade would kill a man each time it was drawn, never rust, and bring about three great evils. Hervör raised it from the barrow of her dead father Angantýr, and the curse worked ruin on every bearer after.
source: Hervarar saga ok Heiðreks

name: Þjófastafur
powers: Protects livestock and goods from thieves.
description: Þjófastafur, the thief stave of the Huld manuscript, drawn to guard livestock and goods against theft. The name means 'thief-stave', and the sign was meant to make a thief unable to take what belonged to the bearer. It answered a real fear in the farmsteads, protecting herds and households that had no other defence.
source: Huld manuscript (Lbs 4626 8vo, 1860)

name: Troll Porridge Bowl
powers: Appeases the tomte so the farm prospers.
description: At Christmas, Swedish farm families set out a bowl of rice porridge with butter for the tomte, the farm's household spirit. The bowl was left in the attic, the barn, or by the hearth; if the butter was hidden or the porridge forgotten, the tomte was said to abandon the farm or work mischief. The custom, documented across Sweden into the twentieth century, is the subject of many tomte tales.
source: Swedish Christmas custom and tomte tales

name: The Troll's Mitten
description: A mitten that a troll or giant is said to have dropped and left behind, so large that a human could use it for shelter or sleep inside the thumb. The motif of the lost glove or mitten of the troll folk appears in Swedish tales as proof of the hidden people's size, and finding it is both marvellous and dangerous.
source: Swedish troll-tale motif of the lost mitten

name: The Troll Shoes
maker: Worn by a troll in the tale
powers: Let the wearer stride over mountains or move faster than thought.
description: Shoes worn by a troll in a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Troll Shoes', the troll's footwear, or the wearing of it, lets a human stride over mountains or move faster than thought, and the shoes are won or put on during the tale's test. The troll's shoes are a typical wonder-object of Swedish troll tales.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Troll Shoes'

name: The Treasure in Säby Creek
description: A hidden treasure said to lie in a creek at Säby in Småland, at the centre of a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Treasure in Säby Creek', the buried hoard is guarded or hard-won, and the treasure-seekers' venture into the creek tests their courage and luck. It belongs to the large Swedish family of tales about treasure guarded in the landscape.
source: Småland folktale 'The Treasure in Säby Creek'

name: Trollkors
powers: Keeps trolls and malevolent powers out of buildings and off objects.
description: A protective cross carved, cut, or forged onto a building, door, or object to stop trolls and harmful powers from harming people or livestock. Documented chiefly in Uppland, Sweden, with similar marks on Norwegian medieval buildings, the crosses were set over doorways and windows and on cookware and loaves of bread. A looped-iron amulet from Dalarna in the 1990s became a tourist talisman.
source: Scandinavian folk protection marks (Nils Ålenius, Uppland)

name: Tune Rune Stone
description: The oldest known Norwegian runestone, found in pieces at Tune in Østfold and dated to around 400 CE. Its short inscription in the early runic alphabet records how heirs divided a man's estate and is among the earliest attestations of a Germanic language. The archaic word forms make it a key document for scholars of early Norse language and runic writing.
source: Runic inscription, Tune, Østfold

name: Troll's Gold
powers: Gifts of troll gold bring luck when accepted with grace and ruin when taken greedily.
description: In Norwegian legend, gold the trolls leave or press on humans, coins, rings, and bracelets that seem to be treasure. Such gold is often said to turn to leaves, shavings, or stone at dawn unless the finder keeps silence or is grateful. The tales warn that grasping after troll treasure brings misfortune, while freely given treasure could bless a whole household.
source: Norwegian folk legend tradition (sagn collections)

name: Trolls' Cast Stones
powers: Boulders said to have been hurled by trolls in anger or dropped in flight.
description: Large scattered boulders that Norwegian legend says trolls hurled in anger, or dropped while fleeing from the sound of church bells. Almost every valley names its stray blocks, the stones of this or that troll woman, and many show the supposed imprint of a giant hand or heel. Geologists read the same boulders as glacial erratics, and the two explanations coexisted for centuries.
source: Norwegian folk legend tradition

name: The Tinderbox
powers: Striking it summons three dogs that fetch treasure, a princess, and rescue from prison.
description: The magic flint and tinder of Hans Christian Andersen's tale, in which a soldier finds an old witch's tinderbox in a hollow tree guarded by three enormous dogs. Each strike of the flint summons one of the dogs, which bring him money, the princess, and rescue from prison. The story, built on older folk motifs of the magic object, turned the homely tinderbox into the key to wealth and a kingdom.
source: Hans Christian Andersen, Fyrtøjet (1835)

name: Trundholm Sun Chariot
powers: A cult object showing the sun drawn across the sky by a horse.
description: A Bronze Age cult figure found in the Trundholm bog on Zealand, Denmark, in 1902: a bronze horse pulling a gilded bronze disc, all mounted on a six-wheeled stand. It is read as the sun drawn across the sky on its daily journey, the oldest such sun-horse image in Nordic art. The chariot is now in the National Museum of Denmark and has become a national symbol.
source: Bronze Age bog find, Trundholm, Zealand (1902)

name: The Tallow Candle
powers: Burns with a clear flame when it finds its purpose.
description: The tallow candle of a Danish poem credited to a young Hans Christian Andersen and found in the national archive in 2012. In the poem a rough, unlit candle complains that it has never burned, until it finds its true use and gives light. The discovery pushed the start of Andersen's literary career back to the early 1820s, and the poem is treated as his earliest known work.
source: Hans Christian Andersen, Tællelyset (c. 1822, found 2012)

name: Talos
powers: Patrolled Crete hurling rocks at ships; kept a single vein of ichor sealed by a nail at the ankle.
description: Talos, the bronze automaton forged by Hephaestus and given to Minos to patrol the shores of Crete; a giant man of bronze with a single vein of ichor sealed by a nail at the ankle. In the Argonautica he hurls rocks at passing ships until Medea charms him and the plug is drawn, draining his life-fluid.
source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica

name: Sword of Theseus
maker: Aegeus (left beneath the rock at Troezen)
powers: Proof of royal birth; recognizes Theseus to his father Aegeus at Athens.
description: The sword of the Athenian hero Theseus, left with a pair of sandals beneath a great rock at Troezen by his father Aegeus; when Theseus grew strong enough to lift the rock, the tokens proved his royal birth, and he carried the sword to Athens, where his father recognized him by it. Plutarch and Pausanias record the tokens.
source: Plutarch, Life of Theseus; Pausanias, Description of Greece

name: Tizona
material: Iron and steel blade with silver-gilt hilt
maker: Blade of Andalusian manufacture, c. 11th century
powers: Sword of El Cid won from King Yucef of Valencia; 'worth a thousand marks of gold' in the Cantar.
description: The sword Tizona, named in the Cantar de Mio Cid as El Cid's blade won from King Yucef of Valencia; the sword shown in the Museo de Burgos has an 11th-century blade, though its hilt and inscriptions are later additions, so its link to Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar rests on legend rather than proof.
source: Cantar de Mio Cid; Museo de Burgos (provenance and metallurgical studies)

name: Talismanic Shirt
material: Cotton or linen, painted with ink and gold
powers: Worn next to the skin to shield the wearer from wounds, illness, and evil in battle.
description: The tilsimli gomlek, or talismanic shirt, a cotton garment painted with Qur'anic verses, magic squares, and astrological signs, worn next to the skin by Ottoman sultans for protection in battle; some eighty survive in the Topkapi collection, including Cem Sultan's shirt begun in 1477, whose astrological moment of making is inscribed in it.
source: Topkapi Palace Museum collection; Tezcan, Tilsimli Gomlekler

name: Tara Brooch
material: Silver-gilt, gold filigree, amber and glass
description: The Tara Brooch, a richly filigreed silver-and-gold annular brooch made around the eighth century. It was discovered in 1850 on the beach at Bettystown, County Meath, and the name 'Tara' was attached for sale because of the site's royal associations. It survives in the National Museum of Ireland with its original chain intact.
source: National Museum of Ireland; 1850 find

name: Tarnhelm
powers: Rendered the wearer invisible.
description: Tarnhelm, the magic cap of invisibility in the Nibelungenlied. Siegfried takes it from the dwarf Alberich along with the Nibelung hoard; it lets him work unseen. Richard Wagner later gave the name to the golden ring's forging helmet in the Ring cycle, where it also allows shape-shifting, a power absent from the medieval poem.
source: Das Nibelungenlied

name: The Temple Menorah
powers: The seven-branched lampstand kept alight in the sanctuary.
description: The seven-branched golden lampstand of the Tabernacle and later of the Jerusalem Temple, prescribed in the Book of Exodus as a beaten-gold work with almond-shaped cups and blossoms, kept burning in the sanctuary. Its image survives on the Arch of Titus relief and throughout Jewish art, and its fate after the Temple's destruction in 70 CE became a theme of Jewish legend and diaspora memory.
source: Book of Exodus; Arch of Titus relief

name: The Tunisian Fibula
powers: Fastened the shawl and served as a bridal heirloom and protective talisman.
description: The large silver pin or brooch, often triangular with a central coral or enamel stud and a long pointed pin, worn by Amazigh women across Tunisia, Algeria, and Morocco to fasten the shawl and passed down as a bridal heirloom. Its form echoes Roman-era brooches of the region, and its silver and coral decoration is documented in museum collections of Maghrebi dress.
source: Museum collections of Maghrebi dress

name: Thuan Thien Sword
powers: Granted victory over the Ming invaders
description: The magic sword Thuan Thien ('Heaven's Will') given to the farmer-emperor Le Loi by the golden turtle god Kim Qui during his revolt against Ming rule. After his victory the turtle surfaced on Hoan Kiem Lake to reclaim the blade, giving the lake its name, the Lake of the Returned Sword.
source: Hoan Kiem Lake legend cycle

name: The Relic of That Phanom
powers: Focus of veneration; guardian presence of the Mekong
description: The relic of the Buddha's breastbone enshrined at That Phanom on the Mekong, the most revered stupa of Laos and northeastern Thailand. Lao legend holds that a naga king, Phanya Sithan, invited the monks and guarded the shrine site, binding the sacred chedi to the river's serpentine protectors.
source: That Phanom legend cycle

name: Tsagaan Tug
powers: Ensign of khanly authority and national unity
description: The white standard (tsagaan tug) that Mongol tradition honors as the ensign of Genghis Khan's lineage, kept at the mausoleum complex in Ordos and paraded with the nine black banners at the Naadam festival. Its horsehair crown and spear shaft mark the enduring authority of the steppe khans.
source: Mongol standard tradition; Naadam ceremony

name: Temalacatl
powers: Center of the gladiatorial sacrifice ritual.
description: A great round stone disk set flat at the plaza where Aztec gladiatorial sacrifice took place. A captive tied to its central hole fought armed warriors one after another, the combat described at length by Bernal Díaz, who watched in Tenochtitlan. The best-known survivor, the Stone of Tizoc, is carved with that ruler's conquests and was recovered in Mexico City's cathedral plaza in 1791.
source: Bernal Díaz del Castillo and the Stone of Tizoc

name: Teponaztli
material: Hollow carved log with two tongues
powers: Speaks the voice of the gods at temple ritual.
description: A hollowed log drum struck with rubber-tipped mallets, its top carved with an H-shaped slit that produces two pitches, played at Aztec festivals, dances and war ceremonies. Spanish chroniclers noted how its deep tones carried across Tenochtitlan, and codices show pairs of players beside the huehuetl in temple courtyards. Fray Bernardino de Sahagún recorded the instrument in detail.
source: Florentine Codex (Sahagún) and early accounts

name: Tzompantli
material: Carved stone rack with wooden poles
powers: Displays the skulls of the sacrificed to the sun.
description: A rack of poles threaded with the skulls of sacrificial victims, erected beside Aztec temple platforms; the name means 'skull rack.' Spanish chroniclers Andrés de Tapia and Bernal Díaz both described the great tzompantli of Tenochtitlan and counted its skulls in the tens of thousands. A stone example still stands beside the Templo Mayor, and similar racks appear in earlier Maya art.
source: Spanish chroniclers and the Templo Mayor excavation

name: Totem Pole
era: Northwest Coast tradition to the present
powers: Proclaims clan lineage and stories in carved cedar.
description: Towering poles carved from whole cedar trunks by Northwest Coast peoples, raised before houses to proclaim lineage, honor the dead, or tell the stories of founding ancestors and the beings who helped them. The figures are not idols but crests and histories, read by those who know them. Colonial bans interrupted carving; the art revived in the twentieth century as a symbol of regional identity.
source: Northwest Coast oral tradition and historical accounts

name: Thunderbird Club
powers: Carries the strike of the thunderbird into battle.
description: A heavy carved club whose grip and head are shaped as a bird, most often the thunderbird, so that each blow falls with the power of the being who makes the thunder and carries lightning. Carried by chiefs and warriors, the club combines weapon and emblem, its carved beak and wings binding the bearer to the great sky bird of the origin stories. Surviving examples are treasured in museums.
source: Northwest Coast and Plains oral tradition

name: Three Sisters Garden
culture: Haudenosaunee and other Eastern Woodlands peoples
material: Interplanted corn, beans and squash in mounds
powers: The three crops support each other as the sisters did the people.
description: The Haudenosaunee method of planting corn, beans and squash together in one mound, each crop helping the others: corn gives the beans a pole, beans fix the soil, and squash shades the roots. The three are called sisters in the peoples' stories, inseparable companions who arrived with the ancestors. The system fed the confederacy, and its lessons in companion planting are studied by farmers today.
source: Haudenosaunee oral tradition and agricultural history

name: Tumi
powers: Sacrificial blade of the priests under the moon.
description: The tumi is the crescent-bladed ceremonial knife of the Andes, a wide arched gold blade on a decorated handle, crafted by the Lambayeque/Sicán culture and later carried into Inca ritual and sacrifice. The most famous example, the Tumi of Lambayeque, was found at Batán Grande in 1936 and has become a national symbol of Peru, reproduced in folk art and worn as an emblem of identity.
source: Lambayeque/Sicán and Inca archaeological finds, including the Tumi of Lambayeque (1936)

name: Tupilak
material: Carved bone, ivory, antler or stone
powers: A vengeful spirit assembled to harm an enemy.
description: A figure the Greenlandic Inuit carved from bone, skin or other gathered parts and animated with magic to be sent against an enemy; the tupilak was made in secret and had to be defeated by its victim's own power or by finding its maker. Carving it was the dangerous part, and today the word names both the spirit and the grotesque figurines that have become Greenlandic art.
source: Greenlandic oral tradition and ethnographic records

name: Tuareg Takuba Sword
description: The takuba is the straight-bladed, cross-hilted sword of the Tuareg of the Sahel, carried by warriors and today worn as a mark of honour. Forged iron blades are paired with decorated leather scabbards, often dyed and embossed. The takuba historically signalled the status of its bearer and featured in Tuareg duels and raids.
source: Tuareg warrior tradition; museum collections

name: Teke Kidumu Mask
description: Teke 'kidumu' masks of the Republic of the Congo are flat, round wooden face masks decorated with painted geometric designs in red, white, and black. Worn by men of the kidumu society at initiations and funerals, the mask's patterns are said to allude to the Teke origin story of a great turtle from whose back the world grew.
source: Teke oral tradition; museum collections

name: Tizerzai Brooch
powers: Fastens the dress and is worn for protection, with engraved motifs said to avert harm.
description: The tizerzai is a large silver brooch of the Amazigh women of Morocco, a crescent- or triangle-shaped clasp used to fasten the shoulder of the dress, fitted with a long pin and decorative chainwork. It is both a practical garment fastener and a piece of protective jewellery, often engraved and embellished with coral or enamel.
source: Amazigh jewellery tradition

name: Tunisian Chechia Cap
description: The chechia is the brimless, red felt cap of Tunisia, traditionally made by hand-felting wool and dyeing it crimson, then shaping it over a wooden mould. Worn by men across the Maghreb as a mark of Tunisian identity, it was produced in the chechia craft quarter of Tunis and given as a gift of distinction.
source: Tunisian craft tradition; historical accounts

name: Trishula of Shiva
description: Three-pronged spear sacred to Shiva, the destroyer, whose prongs stand for creation, preservation and destruction, or for the three gunas that compose the world. Shiva carries the trishula in Puranic sculpture and story, and devotees plant iron trishulas at cremation grounds and shrine thresholds, where the weapon is said to pierce ignorance and drive away evil spirits.
source: Shiva Purana and Shaiva iconographic tradition

name: Tandoor
description: Cylindrical clay oven sunk into the earth or a hearth, fired from below so breads and meats cook against its hot walls, used across North India and the Punjab plains. In village households the tandoor is a shared daily fixture, and its flames carry a homely, auspicious aura; flatbreads are pressed by hand against the clay and baked in seconds.
source: North Indian domestic culinary tradition

name: Tabla
description: Pair of small hand drums, the larger metal-bodied bayan and the smaller wooden dayan, tuned together and played with fingers and palms, central to Hindustani classical rhythm. Tabla playing is learned through rhythmic syllables such as dha, tin and na, and the instrument anchors devotional song and dance, carrying the beat of both court music and folk performance.
maker: tabla makers of Delhi and Banaras
source: Hindustani musicological tradition and instrument history

name: Tulwar
description: Curved single-edged sword of the Indian subcontinent, a cavalry blade with a distinctive hilt whose disc pommel and crossguard appear in tales of Rajput and Mughal warriors. The tulwar was carried as both weapon and emblem of rank, and folk tales of battles, honour and oath-taking treat the sword as a binding object passed down as an heirloom of warrior families.
source: Arms museum collections and court chronicles

name: Thangka
description: Painted or embroidered scroll of Buddhist deities and mandalas, framed in silk and hung in Tibetan Buddhist monasteries and homes of the Himalayan world. Thangkas are painted with mineral pigments to exact iconographic rule, and the images are regarded as aids to meditation and carriers of the blessing of the figures they depict.
material: cotton or silk, mineral pigments, gold
source: Himalayan Buddhist painting tradition

name: Tjurunga
description: Sacred carved board or stone of the Arrernte and other central Australian peoples, engraved with the designs of the Dreaming and treated as the physical body of an ancestor spirit. Kept in secret men's storehouses and brought out for initiation and ceremony, a tjurunga is handed down as a bond between the living, the land and the ancestral beings, its power bound to the pattern carved upon it.
maker: Ancestral law keepers of the Arrernte
source: Spencer and Gillen ethnographic records; Arrernte tradition

name: Tewhatewha
description: Long-handled fighting staff of the Māori, tipped with a shaped blade of wood and often hung with a bunch of feathers or dog-hair at the base of the handle. Used in training and in battle, the tewhatewha was swung in sweeping strikes and could be thrown, and it appears in war dances and chiefly display as a mark of martial skill.
source: Ethnographic accounts of Māori weaponry

name: Toki Poutangata
description: Ceremonial adze of the Māori, fitted with a greenstone or basalt blade lashed to a carved wooden handle and mounted with a plait of fibre and feathers. The toki poutangata was a symbol of chiefly authority, raised in speeches and carried before a rangatira, and the finest blades were treasured heirlooms passed down through the great lineages.
material: pounamu or basalt blade, carved wood, fibre
maker: Māori carvers of the adze tradition
source: Ethnographic scholarship on Māori ceremonial objects

name: Trobriand Yam House (Bwaima)
description: Ornate storehouse of the Trobriand Islands of Papua New Guinea, raised on posts with a steeply pitched roof and decorative woven friezes. The bwaima stores yams, the central wealth and prestige crop, and a man's status is read in the size and beauty of his yam house, which is built to display abundance as the symbolic face of his household.
source: Anthropological studies of the Trobriand Islands

name: Tabua (Whale Tooth)
description: Polished sperm whale tooth of Fiji, presented at weddings, funerals and reconciliation as the highest mark of respect and goodwill. The tabua is offered with a formal speech and is kept by the recipient to seal the covenant, and its giving seals covenants between chiefs, so that a request carried with a tabua is rarely refused.
source: Ethnographic studies of Fijian ceremonial exchange

name: Tongan Ngatu (Barkcloth)
description: Barkcloth of Tonga, made by beating the inner bark of the hiapo tree and pasting the strips together into large sheets painted with stencil patterns in brown and black. Ngatu is produced by women in working parties and given at weddings, funerals and royal ceremonies, and the largest ceremonial pieces are presented to the king.
source: Ethnographic records of Tongan material culture

name: Tahitian Vaʻa (Outrigger Canoe)
description: Ocean-going sailing canoe of the Tahitians, built with a single outrigger float and a lateen sail of matting that carried voyagers across the Pacific. The vaʻa was the vessel of the great Polynesian navigators, who read the stars and swells to settle islands, and it remains raced in the sport of vaʻa today, each hull shaped with the inherited knowledge of the builders.
source: Ethnographic scholarship on Polynesian voyaging

name: Tuvaluan Paopao (Fishing Canoe)
description: Small sailing canoe of the Tuvaluan islands, fitted with a single outrigger and a triangular sail, used for fishing on the lagoon and the open reef. The paopao was built by hand from the island timbers and lashed with sennit, and its design was carried across the atolls by the same navigational knowledge that tied the Pacific peoples together.
source: Ethnographic records of Tuvaluan seafaring
